name: Closed vapor-compression refrigeration
summary: A closed vapor-compression refrigerator evaporates a fluid to absorb heat, then compresses and condenses it for reuse; a Harrison–Siebe ether machine was sold to a London brewery in 1857.
description: A volatile fluid evaporates at a cooling surface; a mechanical compressor raises vapor pressure, a condenser returns it to liquid, and a regulator sends the liquid back to the evaporator.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.
why: Breweries and ice-makers needed cooling that did not depend on natural ice.

market.note: The configuration can be used or supplied for economic production; the first commercial event is a separate question.

evidence.supports: Reports a Harrison–Siebe machine sold to an unnamed London brewery in 1857.
Identifies the 1857 brewery and paraffin-works machines and describes the associated ether-compression, condenser and evaporator arrangement.
Earlier specification describes an evaporation, mechanical compression, condensation and liquid-return loop.

date.basis: Museums Victoria reports an actual sale to a London brewery in 1857.

events.statement: A Harrison–Siebe ether-compression refrigerating machine was sold to a London brewery in 1857.
events.scope: Harrison–Siebe ether vapor-compression refrigeration machine sold to an unnamed brewery.
events.population: The purchasing London brewery and its staff
events.caveats: A 2011 article reports an 1851 ether prototype installation at a Bendigo brewery, but cites a 2004 retrospective; another institutional history dates a Bendigo installation to 1860. It is not established whether these refer to the same machine or whether the 1851 prototype was in brewery use. Twining’s own machine operated intermittently in Cleveland from 1855 according to a 1902 retrospective; its status as experimental versus a broader customer use is unresolved. The 1857 sale is a local transaction, not a claim of worldwide first sale or invention. Perkins’s 1834 patent and 1835 demonstration precede it.
